Beyond Semantic IDs: Atomic Creator Tokens for Large-Scale Generative Recommendation

Zhuosheng Liu Affiliation: Meta Platforms, Menlo Park, CA, USA    Yihan Wu Affiliation: Meta Platforms, Menlo Park, CA, USA    Ziyun Xu Affiliation: Meta Platforms, Menlo Park, CA, USA    Xiaoxuan Liu Affiliation: Meta Platforms, Menlo Park, CA, USA    Longfei Yun Affiliation: Meta Platforms, Menlo Park, CA, USA    Kevin Han Affiliation: Meta Platforms, Menlo Park, CA, USA    Mingze Gao Affiliation: Meta Platforms, Menlo Park, CA, USA    Pengfei Wang Affiliation: Meta Platforms, Menlo Park, CA, USA    Junfeng Pan Affiliation: Meta Platforms, Menlo Park, CA, USA    Wenjie Fu Affiliation: Meta Platforms, Menlo Park, CA, USA    Haoran Liu Affiliation: Meta Platforms, Menlo Park, CA, USA Corresponding author
Abstract

Recommending creators that a user does not yet follow is a cold-start problem: from hundreds of thousands of popular creators and only a short trail of prior engagements, the system must predict the next creator worth surfacing. The prevailing generative recommendation recipe tokenizes each creator into a Semantic ID (SID) by quantizing a frozen embedding and trains a language model to generate SIDs. We show that this SID layer, not the language model, is the binding constraint. The creator-to-SID map is many-to-one, so colliding creators must be resolved by a popularity tie-break that caps creator-level recall and favors already-popular creators, and the frozen quantizer stops the training gradient from reaching the creator representation. We propose Atomic Creator Token (ACT), which gives every creator its own vocabulary token trained end-to-end. The map is bijective, so collisions are impossible and inference is a direct top-kk over creator logits. In a controlled comparison on production data in which the token layer is the only variable, ACT improves creator-level Recall@15 by 19.8 points (1.84×1.84\times) over a matched SID baseline, still leads when the SID codebook is enlarged 64×64\times, and serves at ∼2.7×{\sim}2.7\times lower per-user latency. The advantage carries over to the public KuaiRand dataset, where ACT is the only method that beats a global-popularity baseline, provided each creator token sees enough training examples. In a live A/B test, ACT is directionally positive on every reported metric against both the SID-enhanced and the classic production rankers.

1 Introduction

Recommending creators that a user does not already follow, i.e., unconnected creator recommendation, is a cold-start problem at ecosystem scale. Out of a multi-million catalog, the system must pick from hundreds of thousands of popular creators the few a user will enjoy, with no follower connection and only a short, sparse trail of prior engagements (opens, dwells, follows) on previously suggested creators. Because this signal is so limited, how the model represents creators largely determines what it can recommend. We focus on the head of the catalog, the creators above a follower threshold that a platform can realistically promote and where engagement concentrates: as the head vocabulary grows it covers a rapidly rising share of engagement, so a larger head vocabulary delivers more effective recall (Section 4.4).

The dominant generative recipe, exemplified by OneRec (Deng et al., 2025) and the Transformer Index for Generative Recommenders (TIGER) (Rajput et al., 2023), recasts recommendation as sequence generation over Semantic IDs (SIDs). A pretrained graph neural network (GNN) or two-tower model produces a frozen creator embedding, which residual quantization (Douze et al., 2025) compresses into a short sequence of codebook indices; a language model is then fine-tuned to generate the next SID, and the generated SIDs are decoded back to creators through a codebook join and a popularity rerank.

We argue that this SID layer, not the language model, is the binding constraint, for two compounding reasons. First, the creator-to-SID map is surjective: the used code space is far smaller than the catalog, so many creators share one SID. Even a model that predicts the right SID must still guess which of its creators the user wants, and the popularity tie-break that resolves this guess caps creator-level recall and favors already-famous creators, the opposite of what surfacing fresh creators requires. Second, the quantizer is frozen and non-differentiable: the next-token gradient never reaches the creator representation, so the tokenizer and the language model optimize mismatched objectives. The same design also forces a codebook rebuild for every new creator and a multi-step decode-and-join at serving time.

We therefore propose Atomic Creator Token (ACT), which removes the SID layer entirely (Figure 1). ACT expands the language model’s vocabulary with one dedicated token per candidate creator, up to 30​Y30Y tokens in our study, and trains the model end-to-end to generate the next creator token. Because the creator–token map is bijective, collisions are impossible and inference reduces to a direct top-kk over creator logits with no codebook join or popularity rerank. Because the creator embeddings are model parameters, the next-token gradient trains them directly, which also makes on-policy alignment from engagement feasible. The added capacity is modest: a 10​Y×307210Y\times 3072 embedding table in bf16 adds ≈0.6{\approx}0.6 GB.

ACT is not a drop-in replacement for arbitrarily large catalogs. One token per creator needs enough engagement examples per token to learn a useful embedding, and the output softmax grows with the vocabulary, so we position ACT as the head component of a routed recommender: ACT covers every above-threshold creator, whereas a frozen SID codebook reaches only the 86.3%86.3\% with a GNN embedding, and conventional retrieval serves the sparse long tail. Our public-data study makes this premise explicit (Section 4.5). Our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    a diagnosis of the SID bottleneck in cold-start creator recommendation: a surjective creator-to-SID map imposes a collision-limited recall ceiling, and a frozen quantizer blocks end-to-end representation learning;

  2. 2.

    ACT, a generative recommender with a bijective per-creator vocabulary trained end-to-end, which is collision-free and join-free at inference and fits in a single-host memory budget at 30​Y30Y creators;

  3. 3.

    a controlled evaluation on production data in which the token layer is the only variable: ACT improves creator-level Recall@15 by +19.8+19.8 points (1.84×1.84\times) over a matched SID baseline at a 10​Y10Y-creator vocabulary, still leads when the SID codebook is enlarged to (4​X)3(4X)^{3} at 30​Y30Y creators, and is cheaper to serve;

  4. 4.

    a replication on the public KuaiRand dataset, together with an analysis of when ACT helps: it wins once each creator token has enough training examples, and a live A/B test that is directionally positive on every reported metric.

2 Method

We first define the task and the SID baseline that ACT replaces (Section 2.1), then describe ACT’s tokenization and objective (Section 2.2) and its training pipeline (Section 2.3).

2.1 Task and Semantic-ID Generation

Task.

Let 𝒰\mathcal{U} be the set of users and 𝒜\mathcal{A} the set of candidate creators. Each user u∈𝒰u\in\mathcal{U} has profile features xux_{u} (country, language, gender, age) and a chronological engagement history Htu=((a1,τ1),…,(at,τt))H^{u}_{t}=\big((a_{1},\tau_{1}),\dots,(a_{t},\tau_{t})\big), where ai∈𝒜a_{i}\in\mathcal{A} is the ii-th engaged creator and τi\tau_{i} its engagement type (open, like, share, follow, or long dwell). An engagement-value function v⁡(τ)≥0v(\tau)\geq 0 scores these types, increasing from a brief open to a follow; we use it to weight NDCG and to shape rewards. The task is next-creator prediction: a model Pθ​(at+1∣Htu,xu)P_{\theta}(a_{t+1}\mid H^{u}_{t},x_{u}) with parameters θ\theta returns the KK highest-scoring creators 𝒜^iK\widehat{\mathcal{A}}^{K}_{i} for each test instance ii, and we report

Recall@K=1N∑i=1N[ai⋆∈𝒜^iK],\mathrm{Recall}@K=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\mathbb{1}\!\left[a^{\star}_{i}\in\widehat{\mathcal{A}}^{K}_{i}\right], (1)

where NN is the number of test instances, ai⋆a^{\star}_{i} is the ground-truth next creator of instance i=1,…,Ni=1,\dots,N, and 𝟙​[⋅]\mathbb{1}[\cdot] is the indicator function.

Semantic IDs.

The SID baseline maps each creator to an embedding with a pretrained, frozen encoder E:𝒜→ℝdEE:\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{E}} (a GNN) and quantizes it with LL codebooks, each holding MM centroids {𝐞ℓ,k}k=1M\{\mathbf{e}_{\ell,k}\}_{k=1}^{M}, by greedily quantizing successive residuals:

r(0)=E⁡(a),sℓ​(a)=arg⁡mink∈[M]⁡‖r(ℓ−1)−𝐞ℓ,k‖2,r(ℓ)=r(ℓ−1)−𝐞ℓ,sℓ​(a),r^{(0)}=E(a),\qquad s_{\ell}(a)=\arg\min_{k\in[M]}\big\|r^{(\ell-1)}-\mathbf{e}_{\ell,k}\big\|_{2},\qquad r^{(\ell)}=r^{(\ell-1)}-\mathbf{e}_{\ell,s_{\ell}(a)}, (2)

where dEd_{E} is the embedding dimension, r(ℓ)r^{(\ell)} is the residual left after level ℓ=1,…,L\ell=1,\dots,L, 𝐞ℓ,k\mathbf{e}_{\ell,k} is the kk-th centroid of codebook ℓ\ell, and [M]={1,…,M}[M]=\{1,\dots,M\}. The SID of creator aa is s⁡(a)=(s1​(a),…,sL​(a))∈[M]Ls(a)=(s_{1}(a),\dots,s_{L}(a))\in[M]^{L}, and

ν⁡(s)=|{a∈𝒜:s⁡(a)=s}|\nu(s)=\big|\{a\in\mathcal{A}:s(a)=s\}\big| (3)

is the collision count of code ss, the number of creators that share it. Because the reachable code space is effectively far smaller than |𝒜||\mathcal{A}|, the map ss is surjective and ν⁡(s)>1\nu(s)>1 for many codes.

Generation and inference.

A language model generates the LL code tokens of the next SID autoregressively, Pθ​(s∣H,x)=∏ℓ=1LPθ​(sℓ∣s<ℓ,H,x)P_{\theta}(s\mid H,x)=\prod_{\ell=1}^{L}P_{\theta}(s_{\ell}\mid s_{<\ell},H,x), and is trained with supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Its gradient stops at the SID-token embeddings, so neither EE nor the codebooks adapt to the recommendation objective. At inference, beam search produces candidate SIDs, each SID is expanded to its ν⁡(s)\nu(s) creators by a codebook join, and a popularity score breaks the ties before the top-KK creators are returned.

2.2 Atomic Creator Tokens

ACT keeps this generative setup but removes the SID layer. It assigns each creator a unique token through a bijection ϕ:𝒜→{0,1,…,NA−1}\phi:\mathcal{A}\to\{0,1,\dots,N_{A}-1\}, where NA=|𝒜|N_{A}=|\mathcal{A}|, and expands the base vocabulary 𝒱\mathcal{V} of the language model with the creator tokens {⟨aj⟩}j=0NA−1\{\langle a_{j}\rangle\}_{j=0}^{N_{A}-1}. Whereas the SID map has ν⁡(s)≥1\nu(s)\geq 1, ACT has ν≡1\nu\equiv 1: no two creators share a token, and decoding a token back to a creator is an O⁡(1)O(1) lookup ϕ−1\phi^{-1} instead of a one-to-many codebook join.

Model.

We use a Llama-3.2-3B backbone (Grattafiori et al., 2024) with hidden size d=3072d=3072. Each creator token adds one ordinary vocabulary embedding 𝐰ϕ⁡(a)∈ℝd\mathbf{w}_{\phi(a)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, no different in kind from the model’s word-piece embeddings. A context z=(xu,Htu)z=(x_{u},H^{u}_{t}) is serialized into a prompt, with the profile as text and the history as the sequence of the engaged creators’ tokens, and the backbone fθf_{\theta} produces the hidden state 𝐡=fθ​(z)∈ℝd\mathbf{h}=f_{\theta}(z)\in\mathbb{R}^{d} at the position that predicts the next creator. With decoding restricted to creator tokens, the next-creator distribution is the usual next-token softmax over 𝒜\mathcal{A}:

Pθ​(a∣z)=exp⁡(𝐰ϕ⁡(a)⊤​𝐡)∑a′∈𝒜exp⁡(𝐰ϕ⁡(a′)⊤​𝐡),P_{\theta}(a\mid z)=\frac{\exp\!\big(\mathbf{w}_{\phi(a)}^{\top}\mathbf{h}\big)}{\sum_{a^{\prime}\in\mathcal{A}}\exp\!\big(\mathbf{w}_{\phi(a^{\prime})}^{\top}\mathbf{h}\big)}, (4)

where a′a^{\prime} ranges over all candidate creators. A creator is thus emitted as a single token rather than an LL-token SID.

Objective.

We train with the next-token cross-entropy on the target creator,

ℒSFT=−𝔼(z,a⋆)​[log⁡Pθ​(a⋆∣z)],\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}=-\mathbb{E}_{(z,a^{\star})}\big[\log P_{\theta}(a^{\star}\mid z)\big], (5)

where the expectation 𝔼\mathbb{E} is over training pairs of a context zz and its ground-truth next creator a⋆a^{\star}. There is no separate creator encoder: assigning each creator a vocabulary token is the entire representational change. Because the creator embeddings live inside the model, the loss updates each of them directly,

∇𝐰jℒSFT=(pj−𝟙[j=ϕ(a⋆)])𝐡,pj=Pθ(ϕ−1(j)∣z),\nabla_{\mathbf{w}_{j}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}=\big(p_{j}-\mathbb{1}[\,j=\phi(a^{\star})\,]\big)\,\mathbf{h},\qquad p_{j}=P_{\theta}\big(\phi^{-1}(j)\mid z\big), (6)

where j=0,…,NA−1j=0,\dots,N_{A}-1 indexes the creator tokens and pjp_{j} is the predicted probability of creator ϕ−1​(j)\phi^{-1}(j). The SID pipeline, in contrast, has a zero gradient with respect to its frozen encoder EE.

Why direct tokens dominate.

An SID is a deterministic, lossy function of its creator, so by the data processing inequality an SID history carries no more information about the next SID than a creator history carries about the next creator. The best next-token loss ACT can reach is therefore no worse than that of any SID scheme, for any vocabulary size.

Contrastive auxiliary loss (optional).

To sharpen the discriminability of creator tokens, an in-batch contrastive term can be added over a batch ℬ\mathcal{B} of context–creator pairs, treating the other creators in the batch as negatives:

ℒcon=−1|ℬ|∑i∈ℬlogexp⁡(𝐡i⊤​𝐰ϕ⁡(ai⋆)/κ)∑j∈ℬexp⁡(𝐡i⊤​𝐰ϕ⁡(aj⋆)/κ),\mathcal{L}_{\text{con}}=-\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{B}}\log\frac{\exp\!\big(\mathbf{h}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{w}_{\phi(a_{i}^{\star})}/\kappa\big)}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{B}}\exp\!\big(\mathbf{h}_{i}^{\top}\mathbf{w}_{\phi(a_{j}^{\star})}/\kappa\big)}, (7)

where 𝐡i\mathbf{h}_{i} and ai⋆a_{i}^{\star} are the hidden state and target creator of pair ii, the index jj runs over the pairs in ℬ\mathcal{B}, and κ>0\kappa>0 is a temperature; training then minimizes ℒSFT+λ​ℒcon\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}+\lambda\mathcal{L}_{\text{con}} with weight λ>0\lambda>0. Our ablation finds that this term does not help (Section 4.7).

2.3 Training Pipeline

Initialization.

By default the new creator rows are initialized randomly, 𝐰ϕ⁡(a)∼𝒩⁡(0,σ02​𝐈)\mathbf{w}_{\phi(a)}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_{0}^{2}\mathbf{I}) with standard deviation σ0=0.02\sigma_{0}=0.02. Optionally, they can be warm-started from the GNN embedding through a learned linear projection 𝐏\mathbf{P}, 𝐰ϕ⁡(a)=𝐏​E​(a)\mathbf{w}_{\phi(a)}=\mathbf{P}\,E(a); unlike the SID codebook, this serves only as an initialization and the embedding remains fully trainable. Creators added later receive new rows without a codebook rebuild.

Stage 1: creator-token warm-up.

With the backbone frozen, we train only the new creator rows on creator descriptions and co-engagement sequences, so that the tokens are grounded before sequential training.

Stage 2: sequential SFT.

We adapt the backbone with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) (Hu et al., 2022) and train the creator rows jointly with ℒSFT\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}} on (profile, history)→\,\to\,next-creator examples.

Stage 3: post-training (optional).

Because the creator tokens are part of θ\theta, the policy πθ​(a∣z)=Pθ​(a∣z)\pi_{\theta}(a\mid z)=P_{\theta}(a\mid z) is differentiable over the true action space 𝒜\mathcal{A}, so it can be aligned from engagement with a value-weighted reward

r(a)=∑τv(τ) 1[(a,τ)∈ℱu],r(a)=\sum_{\tau}v(\tau)\,\mathbb{1}\big[(a,\tau)\in\mathcal{F}_{u}\big], (8)

where ℱu\mathcal{F}_{u} is the set of future (creator, engagement-type) pairs of user uu and the sum runs over engagement types τ\tau. We evaluate Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2023), Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (Shao et al., 2024), and Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) (Hübotter et al., 2026) from the SFT model in Appendix C; none improves on it, so the served model is the Stage-2 SFT model.

3 Related Work

Generative recommendation.

Generative recommendation (Yun et al., 2026; Rajput et al., 2023) has become a compelling alternative to multi-stage filtering pipelines. It builds on a long line of sequential recommenders that model user histories with recurrent, self-attentive, bidirectional, and self-supervised encoders (Hidasi et al., 2016; Kang and McAuley, 2018; Sun et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2020) and, more recently, on large-scale generative transducers that recast ranking as sequence generation (Zhai et al., 2024). A foundational design choice is the item identifier, which must carry both semantic content and collaborative signal (Rajput et al., 2023; Singh et al., 2024). The dominant recipe tokenizes each item into a Semantic ID by discretizing a pretrained embedding into a hierarchy of codes and training a language model to generate them (Rajput et al., 2023; Hou et al., 2023; Jin et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024; Hou et al., 2025). MusicRec (Zhao et al., 2026b) and FusID (Kim et al., 2026) further fuse textual and acoustic signals into the embedding before quantization (Zhu et al., 2026). To make these continuous embeddings usable by a large language model (LLM), vector-quantization techniques (van den Oord et al., 2017; Razavi et al., 2019; Défossez et al., 2023) such as the residual quantized variational autoencoder (RQ-VAE) (Lee et al., 2022) and residual quantization with k-means (RQ-KMeans) (Douze et al., 2025) map each embedding to a tuple of codebook indices. All of these methods place a many-to-one quantizer, fixed while the language model trains, between the item and the language model; ACT removes it.

Preference optimization.

Reinforcement learning (RL) is the standard tool for post-training alignment of LLMs (Guo et al., 2025; Team et al., 2025; Olmo et al., 2025; Jaech et al., 2024; Lambert et al., 2024). Methods that learn from verifiable rewards, such as GRPO (Shao et al., 2024), optimize policy gradients on outcome-level rewards, but sparse scalar feedback complicates credit assignment, and process reward models (Setlur et al., 2024) that supply step-level supervision require an auxiliary model. In recommendation, DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) contrasts preferred and rejected items at the item level, which does not decompose over multi-token SIDs; self-distillation methods (Zhao et al., 2026a; Hübotter et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026) instead let the policy, conditioned on realized feedback, act as its own teacher. Because an ACT creator is a single token, all three apply to ACT directly over the true action space; we find, however, that none improves on SFT in our setting (Appendix C).

4 Experiments

We compare ACT with the SID pipeline on production unconnected-creator data and on the public KuaiRand dataset. We ask whether ACT improves creator-level recall (Section 4.2), why (Section 4.3), how vocabulary size trades conditional recall against coverage (Section 4.4), whether the result transfers to public data and when it holds (Section 4.5), what each token layer costs to serve (Section 4.6), which design choices matter (Section 4.7), and whether the offline gain carries over online (Section 4.8).

4.1 Experimental Setup

Production data.

Next-creator examples come from engagements with suggested, non-followed creators (opens, likes, shares, follows, and dwell), with auxiliary cross-surface engagement as additional context and each history truncated to the most recent engaged creators. We split by day so that no test interaction is seen in training, and the target is the next unconnected creator on any surface. We evaluate three nested candidate sets by decreasing follower threshold: top (NA=YN_{A}{=}Y), mid (NA=10​YN_{A}{=}10Y), and broad (NA=30​YN_{A}{=}30Y), so a larger vocabulary adds coverage rather than replacing creators. Vocabulary and codebook sizes are reported in relative units: YY is the smallest vocabulary and XX the base per-level codebook size, so the SID codebooks are X3X^{3}, (2​X)3(2X)^{3}, and (4​X)3(4X)^{3}. The 10​Y10Y setting trains on ∼10{\sim}10M engagement events and tests on ∼1{\sim}1M; the other settings use a test set of the same scale.

Public data.

To test transfer, we use KuaiRand-27K (Gao et al., 2022): the task is to predict the next clicked creator from a user’s 20 most recent creators. We restrict the candidate set to the top-50k creators by training clicks (90.4%90.4\% of training clicks), giving 27,065 users, 16.52M training and 100k test examples. Both token schemes use identical samples in identical order and differ only in the creator token; both are trained with Stage 2 only (no warm-up) for one epoch at learning rate 10−410^{-4}. We add two heuristic baselines, global popularity (the most-clicked creators in training) and recent history (the user’s most recent creators). To probe how much data ACT needs, we also train ACT on the smaller KuaiRand-1K, both on all of its creators and on its top creators.

SID baseline.

The SID baseline follows OneRec (Deng et al., 2025): a frozen GNN embedding quantized by RQ-KMeans (L=3L{=}3, M=XM{=}X unless stated) on the same creators, generated by the same backbone, and decoded by codebook join and popularity rerank. Only the token layer differs from ACT.

Metrics.

Because the served unit is a creator, we score both methods by creator-level Recall@KK (K∈{1,5,10,15,50,200}K\in\{1,5,10,15,50,200\}), i.e., whether the true creator is in the top-KK, and by normalized discounted cumulative gain (NDCG@200) weighted by the engagement value v⁡(τ)v(\tau). For ACT a token is a creator. For SID we expand each predicted SID into its member creators, ranked by beam order and then by follower count within a SID. We also report SID cluster-level recall, which counts a hit whenever the predicted SID equals the target’s SID; it overstates delivered recall because one SID stands for ν⁡(s)\nu(s) creators, so only creator-level recall is comparable to ACT.

Implementation.

Stage 1 trains the creator rows for one epoch at learning rate 10−410^{-4}; Stage 2 applies LoRA (rank r=64r{=}64, scaling α=128\alpha{=}128, dropout 0.050.05) with the creator rows trainable, at learning rate 2×10−52\times 10^{-5} with a cosine schedule. Training runs in bf16 with fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP) on 44 hosts ×\times 88 graphics processing units (GPUs); inference uses vLLM over the expanded vocabulary with beam width 1515 for K≤15K{\leq}15 and 200200 for the deeper cutoffs.

4.2 Main Results

ACT outperforms the SID baseline on every reported production metric at the 10​Y10Y scale with the base X3X^{3} codebook. Creator-level Recall@15 rises from 23.58%23.58\% to 43.41%43.41\%, Recall@50 from 34.33%34.33\% to 60.27%60.27\%, and Recall@200 from 47.62%47.62\% to 79.30%79.30\%. The corresponding absolute gains are 19.8319.83, 25.9425.94, and 31.6831.68 percentage points: ACT’s lead is present for short candidate lists and remains substantial for deeper ones. NDCG@200 also increases from 0.1870.187 to 0.3430.343, a relative gain of 83.4%83.4\%, indicating that the recall improvement is accompanied by better performance under the rank-sensitive, engagement-weighted metric. The advantage holds across the vocabulary and codebook settings in Figure 2, where ACT leads at every plotted cutoff (K∈{1,5,10,15}K\in\{1,5,10,15\}) in all four production settings. With the SID codebook fixed at X3X^{3}, ACT achieves Recall@15 of 59.80%59.80\% versus 40.81%40.81\% for SID at YY, and 43.41%43.41\% versus 23.58%23.58\% at 10​Y10Y (Table 1). Both methods have lower conditional recall in the larger vocabulary, but the absolute advantage of ACT stays close to 1919–2020 points. Its relative gain consequently widens from 46.5%46.5\% to 84.1%84.1\%. Enlarging the SID codebook improves the baseline but does not close this gap: at 10​Y10Y, increasing the per-level size from XX to 2​X2X expands the nominal code space eightfold and raises SID Recall@15 from 23.58%23.58\% to 29.21%29.21\%. ACT still reaches 43.41%43.41\%, retaining a 14.2014.20-point advantage. At the broadest 30​Y30Y tier, even the (4​X)3(4X)^{3} codebook, with 6464 times the nominal capacity of X3X^{3}, yields 30.15%30.15\% Recall@15 against ACT’s 38.87%38.87\%. ACT also leads at every smaller plotted cutoff in this setting, so its advantage persists beyond the smallest, most popular creator tier and against codebooks with substantially more capacity. Section 4.3 examines the collision losses behind this pattern, and Appendix A details the broadest-scale comparison and its differing embedding coverage. All these recalls are scored at the creator level, after expanding SID predictions into ranked creators, and thus measure retrieval of the actual target rather than its semantic cluster. Since recall is conditional on the target belonging to each vocabulary, the lower values at larger tiers do not by themselves establish which catalog size is best for all engagement; Section 4.4 evaluates that tradeoff by combining conditional recall with engagement coverage.

4.3 Why Atomic Creator Tokens Beat Semantic IDs

SID predictions must identify a creator after identifying its semantic code, and collisions introduce a loss at this second step. Creator-level recall factorizes as

RcreatorSID=RclusterSID×ρ,ρ∈(0,1],R^{\text{SID}}_{\text{creator}}=R^{\text{SID}}_{\text{cluster}}\times\rho,\qquad\rho\in(0,1], (9)

Here, RcreatorSIDR^{\text{SID}}_{\text{creator}} is SID’s creator-level Recall@15, which counts a hit only when the true creator appears in the final top-15 list. RclusterSIDR^{\text{SID}}_{\text{cluster}} is its cluster-level Recall@15, which counts a hit when the target’s SID is retrieved. ρ=RcreatorSID/RclusterSID\rho=R^{\text{SID}}_{\text{creator}}/R^{\text{SID}}_{\text{cluster}} is the resolution efficiency: the fraction of cluster-level hits retained after expanding the predicted SIDs into creators and applying the popularity tie-break. A value of ρ=1\rho=1 means that this resolution step loses no hits, while a smaller value indicates a larger loss.

Whenever ν>1\nu>1 and the tie-break is not user-specific, ρ<1\rho<1, roughly ρ≲1/ν¯\rho\lesssim 1/\bar{\nu} for mean collision count ν¯\bar{\nu}; ACT has ν≡1\nu\equiv 1 and hence ρ≡1\rho\equiv 1. Thus, even with identical cluster-level accuracy, SID loses a (1−ρ)(1-\rho) fraction of its hits, the collision tax. This is also why SID cluster-level recall can exceed ACT’s creator-level recall while SID is the weaker system: hitting the code does not identify the creator. The measured recalls in Table 1 show that ρ\rho falls from YY to 10​Y10Y as ν¯\bar{\nu} rises under a fixed X3X^{3} codebook. SID is therefore doubly penalized at scale: the code is harder to predict and the tax is heavier, whereas ACT pays only the first cost, which helps explain why its relative advantage widens with the catalog. Increasing the codebook size partly recovers these lost hits. Holding the creators, data, and decoding fixed and varying only the per-level size, (2​X)3(2X)^{3} at 10​Y10Y substantially raises ρ\rho and SID recall, supporting collisions as an important source of the gap, yet ACT still leads (Figure 3). Pushed to 30​Y30Y creators with a 64×64\times larger (4​X)3(4X)^{3} codebook, collisions fall monotonically with codebook size but never reach zero, because the frozen GNN embeddings cluster intrinsically (Appendix A). ACT keeps a clear lead even though SID is scored only on the creators that have a GNN embedding, while ACT is scored on all of them. Enlarging the codebook buys diminishing returns; only ν≡1\nu\equiv 1 removes the tax outright. The learned representations provide a complementary view of the remaining gap. The data processing inequality discussed in Section 2.2 relates SID’s fixed quantization to information loss, while ACT learns its creator embeddings directly under the sequential objective. Consistent with this distinction, the learned creator embeddings are largely decoupled from the frozen GNN prior: global, local, and layout-level agreement measures indicate little shared structure (Appendix D). ACT thus learns a task-specific geometry rather than simply re-deriving the collaborative geometry encoded by the SID quantizer.

\FloatBarrier

4.4 Vocabulary Size and Coverage

A larger vocabulary makes each prediction harder but covers more of what users engage with. As the ACT vocabulary grows from YY to 30​Y30Y, recall conditional on the target being in the vocabulary falls, while the share of engagement the vocabulary covers rises faster, so the effective recall over all engagement increases at every step (Figure 4). Within the head regime, a larger ACT vocabulary is therefore strictly better in delivered recall, which motivates scaling ACT up to the point where per-token data runs out (Section 4.5).

\FloatBarrier

4.5 Public Data: KuaiRand

ACT’s advantage over SID also appears on KuaiRand-27K, where both models use identical training and test samples, the same sample order, and one epoch of Stage 2 training without vocabulary warm-up. ACT leads SID at every evaluated cutoff from K=5K{=}5 (Figure 7): Recall@5 is 1.138%1.138\% versus 0.903%0.903\%, and Recall@15 is 2.763%2.763\% versus 1.859%1.859\%, corresponding to relative gains of 26.0%26.0\% and 48.6%48.6\%. The absolute gap also grows from 0.2350.235 to 0.9040.904 percentage points, so the benefit extends beyond selecting a single creator. The two heuristic baselines provide a useful check on what the models learn. Global popularity is competitive on this task, reaching 2.351%2.351\% Recall@15, while recent history reaches 1.982%1.982\%. ACT exceeds both and is the only method above global popularity at every evaluated cutoff; its relative lift over popularity is 33.7%33.7\% at K=5K{=}5, 21.8%21.8\% at K=10K{=}10, and 17.5%17.5\% at K=15K{=}15. SID, in contrast, falls below global popularity from K=10K{=}10 and also below recent history at K=15K{=}15. Its only advantage over ACT is at K=1K{=}1, where recall is 0.332%0.332\% versus 0.294%0.294\%. This small top-1 lead is consistent with the popularity prior introduced by returning the most popular creator within each predicted SID, but it does not persist as the candidate list grows. The public-data codebook has 1.301.30 creators per SID and a 36.2%36.2\% colliding fraction, close to the collision profile of the production (4​X)3(4X)^{3} codebook. The result therefore holds with a substantially less colliding quantizer than the base production codebook. The learned ACT vocabulary is also used broadly: top-1 predictions span 12,260 distinct creators, compared with 4,399 distinct codes predicted by SID on the same test set. However, the smaller KuaiRand-1K experiments show that atomic tokens do not automatically outperform simple retrieval heuristics. With all creators included, ACT achieves 0.75%0.75\% Recall@15 against 1.76%1.76\% for the best heuristic; restricting the vocabulary to top creators raises ACT recall to 1.86%1.86\%, still below the heuristic’s 3.78%3.78\%. These settings provide about 55 and 3434 training samples per creator token on average, compared with about 331331 in the KuaiRand-27K top-50k setting. The larger dataset also supplies more total training data, so this comparison does not isolate a universal samples-per-token threshold. It does show that the public-data gain depends on the available supervision, rather than following from the one-token representation alone. Together, these results support the routed design of Section 1: use ACT for well-observed creators in the head and conventional retrieval where creator-level training data remains sparse.

\FloatBarrier

4.6 Inference Cost

ACT is also cheaper to serve at every scale (Figure 8). Under the same hardware (32×32\timesA100-80GB), beam width 1515, and ∼1{\sim}1M-user test set, ACT needs less GPU memory per card, serves more concurrent requests at a fixed memory budget, and has lower per-user latency. The driver is one token versus five: SID emits a five-token block (⟨\langlebos⟩s1s2s3⟨\rangle\,s_{1}s_{2}s_{3}\,\langleeos⟩\rangle), which multiplies the decode steps and the key–value (KV) cache held by every beam, whereas the only extra cost of ACT is a wider softmax over the expanded vocabulary, a single bandwidth-friendly matrix multiplication. The token-layer choice is therefore a Pareto improvement in both accuracy and serving cost.

\FloatBarrier

4.7 Ablation Study

GNN warm-starting yields modest recall gains over random initialization (Table 2). Adding the in-batch contrastive auxiliary loss to the warm-started variant reduces recall at every reported cutoff. We use the simpler model with randomly initialized, trainable creator embeddings for serving. Although ACT makes on-policy alignment feasible, none of DPO, GRPO, or SDPO improves on the SFT model (Appendix C), which keeps reinforcement learning off the serving critical path.

\FloatBarrier

4.8 Online Test

We evaluate ACT in a live four-arm A/B test against the SID-enhanced production arm (prod+SID) and the classic production ranker (prod). The ACT arm has a positive directional lift for every reported metric against both controls (Table 3). The largest change is in product engagement: +0.29%+0.29\% over prod+SID and +0.66%+0.66\% over prod, with the latter approaching statistical significance (p≈0.05p\approx 0.05). The other changes are small and are best interpreted as directional evidence that the offline recall gain transfers online.

5 Conclusion

In cold-start unconnected creator recommendation, the binding constraint is the SID layer, not the language model: a surjective creator-to-SID map imposes a collision-limited recall ceiling, and a frozen quantizer blocks end-to-end learning. ACT removes this layer with a bijective per-creator vocabulary trained end-to-end. Under a controlled comparison, ACT improves creator-level Recall@15 by +19.8+19.8 points (1.84×1.84\times) over a matched SID baseline, keeps its lead as the catalog and the codebook grow, transfers to the public KuaiRand dataset, and is cheaper to serve. Its premise is that every creator token sees enough training data, so ACT is best deployed as the head of a routed system, with the long tail served by conventional retrieval. Multi-interest decoding, hierarchical tokens for latency-critical settings, and on-policy alignment for objectives that SFT cannot express are natural next steps.

Appendix A Largest-Scale Codebook Stress Test

Table 4 details the stress test of Section 4.3: a 30​Y30Y-creator catalog with the SID codebook grown from X3X^{3} to (4​X)3(4X)^{3}. Collisions shrink monotonically with codebook size but never vanish: even the largest codebook leaves a large share of creators sharing a code, because the frozen GNN embeddings cluster intrinsically. Against the strongest SID, ACT still leads at every cutoff, and the comparison favors SID, which is scored only on the ∼76%{\sim}76\% of the 30​Y30Y creators that have a GNN embedding, whereas ACT is scored on all of them.

Appendix B Non-Generative Retrieval Baselines

The main text compares ACT with a matched SID model, the representation the generative recipe directly replaces. For completeness, we also place ACT against the non-generative retrieval it would sit next to in a routed system: the deployed creator-to-creator (C2C) retrieval stack. We report two of its live sources (A and B, identities masked) and the reciprocal-rank-fusion (RRF) ensemble C that unions them and is the one actually served. All methods are scored on the same ∼1{\sim}1M-user test set by creator-level Recall@15, conditional on the target falling inside the vocabulary at each scale; the generative models decode with beam width 15, and the retrieval sources return their native ranked lists.

Table 5 shows a clean ladder at every scale. The C2C sources retrieve few in-vocabulary candidates for these unconnected creators, so their recall is coverage-limited by construction. They are general-purpose retrievers tuned for the broad catalog rather than the popularity-scoped head that ACT targets, so the comparison is directional rather than matched. Still, the matched SID model clearly outperforms the best retriever, and ACT leads throughout, which supports reserving conventional retrieval for the long tail.

Appendix C Post-Training

Because ACT’s creator embeddings are policy parameters, the policy πθ​(a∣z)\pi_{\theta}(a\mid z) is differentiable over the true action space, so we ask whether on-policy alignment also helps. We apply three alignment methods to a shared SFT reference policy πref=πθSFT\pi_{\text{ref}}=\pi_{\theta_{\text{SFT}}}, with the value-weighted reward r⁡(a)r(a) of Section 2.3.

DPO

(Rafailov et al., 2023) uses item-level pairs of a preferred creator a+a^{+} and a rejected creator a−a^{-} and minimizes

ℒDPO=−𝔼(z,a+,a−)​[log⁡σ⁡(β​log⁡πθ​(a+∣z)πref​(a+∣z)−β​log⁡πθ​(a−∣z)πref​(a−∣z))],\mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}}=-\mathbb{E}_{(z,a^{+},a^{-})}\!\left[\log\sigma\!\Big(\beta\log\tfrac{\pi_{\theta}(a^{+}\mid z)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(a^{+}\mid z)}-\beta\log\tfrac{\pi_{\theta}(a^{-}\mid z)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(a^{-}\mid z)}\Big)\right], (10)

where σ\sigma is the logistic function, β>0\beta>0 controls the strength of the implicit KL constraint to πref\pi_{\text{ref}}, and the expectation is over contexts with a preference pair.

GRPO

(Shao et al., 2024) samples a group of GG on-policy creators {ai}i=1G∼πθold(⋅∣z)\{a_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(\cdot\mid z) from the previous policy πθold\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}, scores each with reward ri=r⁡(ai)r_{i}=r(a_{i}), and forms group-normalized advantages A^i=(ri−mean⁡(𝐫))/std⁡(𝐫)\hat{A}_{i}=(r_{i}-\mathrm{mean}(\mathbf{r}))/\mathrm{std}(\mathbf{r}) over the group rewards 𝐫=(r1,…,rG)\mathbf{r}=(r_{1},\dots,r_{G}), updating θ\theta with the clipped policy-gradient surrogate and a KL penalty to πref\pi_{\text{ref}}. Because an ACT creator is a single token, the diversity of a group is exactly the entropy of πθ(⋅∣z)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid z): a low-entropy SFT model yields near-duplicate rollouts, std⁡(𝐫)→0\mathrm{std}(\mathbf{r})\to 0, and the advantages, hence the gradient, vanish.

SDPO

(Zhao et al., 2026a; Hübotter et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026) needs no external reward model: it conditions the policy on its own realized engagement feedback ff to form a self-teacher πθ(⋅∣z,f)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid z,f) that supplies dense targets, and trains the student πθ(⋅∣z)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid z) to match it. Its signal is proportional to the teacher–student gap, which collapses when conditioning on ff barely changes the distribution.

Results.

No recipe beats SFT (Table 6). DPO is compared against the main SFT model; GRPO and SDPO run through the on-policy evaluation flow and are compared against its own reference. The best DPO run only matches SFT, and GRPO and SDPO fall below their reference. The cause is structural rather than a tuning artifact: a single-token, low-entropy policy over a 10​Y10Y-way vocabulary yields near-duplicate rollouts and a sparse, low-variance reward, whereas ACT already casts recommendation as dense, exactly labeled token prediction that SFT optimizes directly. For a production system this outcome is welcome: reinforcement learning need not sit on the serving critical path.

Appendix D Representation Analysis: ACT against the GNN Prior

Section 4.3 argued that ACT learns a task-specific creator geometry rather than re-deriving the frozen GNN prior. We test this by comparing the 30723072-dimensional creator-token rows of the 10​Y10Y model with the 128128-dimensional production GNN embeddings of the same 10,00010{,}000 creators, using independent t-SNE projections (Figure 9) and three measures of structural agreement (Table 7).

We use three complementary measures because no single one is decisive. Linear centered kernel alignment (CKA) captures global alignment and is invariant to orthogonal transforms and isotropic scaling, so the dimensionality gap does not bias it. The kk-nearest-neighbor overlap (kNN@10) probes local structure: the fraction of each creator’s ten nearest GNN neighbors that stay among its ten nearest in ACT space. Procrustes disparity, computed on the two t-SNE layouts after the optimal rotation, reflection, and scaling, measures how far the layouts diverge once that freedom is removed. All three would sit near their “identical” end if ACT merely re-derived the GNN prior.

Instead, all three show that the two representations are largely decoupled (Table 7). Global agreement is close to zero; local overlap is well above chance, so a thin residue of collaborative locality survives, yet most of each creator’s GNN neighborhood is reorganized; and after optimal alignment the same creator lands far apart in the two layouts. The two t-SNE panels look superficially similar, a known t-SNE artifact; the quantitative measures, not the pictures, carry the conclusion. The cause is architectural: the creator rows are randomly initialized and learn their own geometry under the sequential objective, whereas an SID model is confined to the geometry the frozen quantizer already encodes.
